intros.market: Five CAs control 93.7% of all publicly trusted certificate issuance. Internet Security Research Group leads at 41.2%, followed by Google Trust Services at 15.2%, DigiCert at 13.8%, GoDaddy at 12.8%, and Sectigo at 10.7%. The three-firm concentration ratio stands at 70.2%, with an HHI of 2420 indicating high market concentration. This dominance by a handful of US-based entities creates systemic dependencies explored in the concentration and geographic risk tabs.
intros.trust: Root programs disagree substantially on which CAs to trust: 335 total roots exist across four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and just 38 CA owners enjoy universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple stores, creating operational complexity where certificate chains trusted in Edge may fail validation in other browsers. These disagreements force CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and complicate incident response, as a distrust action by one program may not be honored by others.
intros.conc: The HHI of 2420 places the WebPKI in high concentration territory, with the top three CAs issuing 70.2% of all certificates and the top five capturing 93.7% of the market. This concentration creates systemic risk: operational failures or compromise at any of these five organizations would affect the majority of encrypted web traffic. While 95 CAs hold trust store inclusion, 80 operate in the long tail with minimal issuance, suggesting the effective market is even more concentrated than raw CA counts indicate.
intros.tail: Eighty CAs collectively issue just 6.35% of all certificates yet maintain full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure. Each of these low-volume operators can compromise any browser or operating system but lacks the operational maturity, audit scrutiny, and incident response capabilities of high-volume issuers. This trust-without-scale dynamic appears in the governance data, where oversight coverage has declined even as the tail persists in root stores.
intros.geo: CAs incorporated in the United States issue 88.9% of all publicly trusted certificates, with European CAs contributing 11.0% and Asia-Pacific operators barely registering at 0.05%. This concentration reflects both the market dominance of US-based CAs and the regional distribution of internet infrastructure. While 48 European CAs hold trust store inclusion, their combined issuance barely exceeds that of DigiCert alone, and the 17 Asia-Pacific CAs issue less than a tenth of a percent despite serving billions of users.
intros.gov: Thirty-one government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but collectively issue just 0.06% of certificates. These entities span multiple jurisdictions including high-risk countries identified in the jurisdiction risk tab, where legal frameworks enable compelled disclosure or surveillance. Their minimal issuance does not eliminate risk: a government CA can issue valid certificates for any domain, and several distrust events have involved state-affiliated operators exhibiting negligent or argumentative noncompliance patterns.
intros.jurisdiction: Five countries present high legal risk for CA operations due to compelled disclosure frameworks, government access requirements, or weak rule of law: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey occupy a moderate-risk tier with evolving data localization and surveillance laws. These jurisdictions overlap with the 31 government-operated CAs in trust stores, and seven of the 16 distrust events involved CAs in high or moderate-risk jurisdictions exhibiting negligent noncompliance or demonstrated incompetence postures.
intros.ops: No incidents were reported in the current observation period, presenting a surveillance gap when compared to audit intelligence findings. Self-detection accounts for only 23% of historical incident discovery, with external researchers finding 19%, automated tools 18%, audits 8%, and root programs 4%. Policy failures and disclosure failures persist in the historical record, but the zero-incident current state likely reflects detection lag rather than perfect compliance, particularly given the governance tab's finding that root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67-78% in 2019 to under 20% in 2025.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture remains stable with near-universal migration to RSA 4096-bit keys and SHA-256 signatures. The few remaining SHA-1 roots exist only for backwards compatibility and do not issue new certificates. ECDSA P-384 adoption continues gradually among newer roots, though RSA dominates due to hardware compatibility requirements. This cryptographic baseline meets current standards but offers little defense against the compliance and operational failures documented in the distrust and incident histories.
intros.distrust: Sixteen distrust events have occurred across the ecosystem's history, with 14 involving compliance or operational failures and 10 showing a pattern of repeated issues. Seven cases exhibited negligent noncompliance, three involved willful circumvention, and three demonstrated incompetence, while argumentative noncompliance appeared twice. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement was 1,185 days, giving affected CAs over three years to transition customers but also prolonging ecosystem exposure to known-bad actors.
intros.policy: Of 43 active TLS CAs measured, only 12 have achieved the 47-day maximum validity readiness required by March 2029, while 4 remain at risk of missing the 200-day threshold already in effect as of March 2026 and 5 more face the 100-day deadline in March 2027. The median observed validity period is 65 days, suggesting most CAs are operationally prepared for nearer-term thresholds but lag on the final target. This readiness challenge exists against a regulatory surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,651 total obligations, of which 5,050 are mandatory requirements spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF standards—an expanding compliance burden that strains even well-resourced operators.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% (Chrome) and 78.0% (Mozilla) in 2019 to 18.4% and 9.9% respectively in 2025, with Apple at 5.4% and Microsoft contributing zero oversight comments. Of 223 incident reports filed in 2025, Chrome commented substantively on just 41 and Mozilla on 22, leaving the majority of compliance failures unexamined by the entities that control trust decisions. This decline occurs even as Chrome has processed 716 total oversight bugs and Mozilla 813, indicating capacity exists but is not deployed, while the 1,738-bug corpus shows declining engagement per incident over time.
intros.community: Fifty-six organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 25 participate actively in standards development, with 31 contributing zero ballot activity. Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, while DigiCert employees collectively dominate organizational contribution metrics. This silent majority pattern means a small group of CAs effectively writes the compliance rules the entire ecosystem must follow, while the 80 long-tail CAs holding trust store inclusion neither shape policy nor receive proportional governance scrutiny.
intros.audit: Eighty-eight CAs have submitted 81 parsed audit letters with 6 qualified opinions, 19 auditor changes in 2025 alone, and only 1 letter using the latest ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5 standard. The audit market itself shows low concentration with an HHI of 496.8 across firms led by KPMG (10 CAs, 71.5 avg quality score), Deloitte (8 CAs, 75.0), and Ernst & Young (6 CAs, 73.3). In-period detection rate data is not available in this observation window, but zero high-transparency-gap findings suggest audit letters and incident histories remain misaligned—clean opinions coexist with the compliance failures that drive the 223 bugs filed in 2025 and the governance coverage collapse documented across root programs.
